contentBody:
Diya built a page for hostel residents who need a roommate to collect a parcel from the guard desk. A tester writes: “I don’t like this feature.”

Which rewrite is a strong test scenario she can actually act on?
option.1: Ask them to rate how pretty the header looks, then add a darker theme, a logo animation, and a longer About page until comments about taste stop.
option.2: Ask “would you use this in future?” and, if they say maybe, pile on ratings, rewards, and a city-wide courier marketplace on the same first screen.
option.3: A hostel resident, late and stressed at Friday 7 pm during class: the guard desk is about to close, nobody on her roommate list is free, and the parcel may go back.
option.4: Copy “I don’t like this feature” into the backlog as a full redesign of every screen so taste complaints never appear again.
answerExplanation:
A test scenario is a short, realistic moment: who is using it and in what mood, when and where they are, what they want, what they see or miss, and the risk if the flow fails. Friday 7 pm, class, a closing desk, an empty roommate list, and a parcel sent back is a moment Diya can test. “This page looks ugly” and “I don’t like this feature” are reactions, not tests.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- A: Looks and brand taste are reactions. Extra polish does not name who, when, the missing action, or the risk.
- B: “Would you use this in future?” invites polite fiction. Bolting on extras still is not a scenario.
- D: Repeating the complaint as a redesign brief keeps the feedback weak. There is still no moment to run.

contentBody:
Aman is testing a canteen “hold my token” request. The core job is: send a request so a friend can collect the token. He also wrote: once the friend starts paying the token fee, that payment should not fail silently.

Which statement is correct?
option.1: Sending the request is a functional need. Finishing without silent failure is reliability — a “how well” test, not a new product line.
option.2: PQRSTU is a shopping list, so Performance, Quality, Reliability, Security, Transparency, and Usability must all ship on day one.
option.3: A non-functional requirement is what the product must do, and a functional requirement is only how colourful the buttons look.
option.4: Security means “can they finish in a few taps,” and Usability means “can a stranger or a scam use this against someone.”
answerExplanation:
A functional requirement is what the product must do (send the hold request). A non-functional requirement is how well it must do it. Reliability asks whether, once started, the action finishes without silent failure. Those “how well” rows become test scenarios. They are not a second product.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- B: Not every PQRSTU row must ship in version one. The framework invents holistic tests. You later select which rows are must-have now.
- C: This swaps the two terms. Functional is the job. Non-functional is speed, scale, safety, honesty, and ease. Colour is not the definition.
- D: Those two lenses are reversed. Usability is few taps without a tutorial. Security is whether a stranger or a scam can use the flow against someone.

contentBody:
Harsh wants to know if his “ask a cousin to pay the coaching-class fee this month” flow helps the intended problem — complete a payment when the student is temporarily short of money.

Which plan is correct?
option.1: Start with “Do you like this?” and “Would you use this in future if we added a nicer logo?” so testers can give polite praise without opening any memory of a real bill.
option.2: Show the prototype immediately, ask “cool, right?”, then ask his mother whether the idea is good, and treat the first compliment as proof that the intended problem is solved.
option.3: Switch the interview to grocery-expense tracking and future predictions, because people are good at guessing whether they will love a product that does not exist yet.
option.4: Ask how the last time they were short actually went, stay in that past until a situation appears, show the flow only then, and let them tap without asking for compliments.
answerExplanation:
The intended problem is the specific pain the offer promised to reduce, not whether people “like” the idea. The useful order is: open-ended questions in the past, stay in the past, keep asking why until you reach a situation rather than a slogan, show the prototype only after they are in that memory, then hand it over. Compliments are not evidence. Listen more than you talk.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- A: “Do you like this?” and “Would you use this in future?” invite polite fiction and skip the real past.
- B: Showing first and asking “is my idea good?” is the opposite of the Mom Test as used here. Talk about their life first, then let them try.
- C: Grocery tracking is a different job. People are bad at predicting the future, so future-love questions are weak.

contentBody:
Isha uses a chat tool to rehearse feedback on her library-slot page. She has three voices ready: someone who actually misses the last slot, someone who would rather shout in the old WhatsApp group, and someone who never uses the library.

What should she do?
option.1: Dump intended, sceptic, and wrong users in one chat and ask for a score out of 10 so she can average them into a single ranking.
option.2: Keep one voice per chat, ask only her five questions, treat replies as rehearsal, and look for patterns herself.
option.3: Invert the mix and call the chatbot a field study of India, because it can invent download numbers, loyalty, and favourite apps.
option.4: Keep only the intended user; sceptic and wrong voices waste time and should never be simulated in separate threads.
answerExplanation:
Simulated user feedback is a model answering as if it were a type of person. The replies are plausible reactions, not real evidence. Mixed context in one chat makes the model blend voices and invent details. Run separate conversations, ask the five questions, do not request a score out of 10, and you look for patterns. A practical mix is about 40% real conversations and 60% simulated iterations — simulation for volume, real people for truth.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- A: One chat plus a score out of 10 is exactly what to avoid. Do not average people into “8/10 liked it.”
- C: The model has no loyalty and no favourite app. Invented download numbers are not a survey. Do not call the chatbot a field study.
- D: Always include intended, sceptic, and wrong. A sceptic could need you and still refuse. A wrong user will never be in that situation. Both are useful if they stay in separate chats.

contentBody:
Three people looked at Kabir’s “ask a sibling to pay the electricity bill” prototype.

- Sana runs out of balance before month-end and will ask her brother.
- Rohan sometimes has the same pinch but would rather take one bulk cash amount than send a small request each time.
- Priya always ends the month in surplus. An investor also asked to “see the deck.”

Which labelling is correct?
option.1: Sana is intended, Rohan is sceptic, Priya is wrong; drop the investor. Sceptic and wrong are not the same type.
option.2: Treat Priya as intended and keep the investor as an extra voice, because surplus money and a funding meeting are the best proof that the electricity-bill job is real.
option.3: Label Rohan and Priya as the same “no” user, then average Sana’s yes with their no into a single 8/10 popularity score for the prototype.
option.4: Put Sana, Rohan, Priya, and the investor in one chat so the model can blend Priya’s surplus with Sana’s pinch and invent a mixed persona.
answerExplanation:
An intended user genuinely has the pain and will try the product. A sceptic sometimes has the pain but prefers the old workaround (bulk cash, self-respect, the WhatsApp plea). A wrong user does not need this by any means — surplus every month. Wrong is not the same as sceptic. An investor, a person shopping for a new credit card, or someone buying mutual funds is not your user. Drop those rows.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- B: Priya will never be in the short-of-money situation. Thank her and leave her out of the MVP story. An investor is not an extra/risk user of this job.
- C: “No” is not one type. Averaging into a popularity score hides motivations and concerns.
- D: Mixing voices in one chat is how the model hallucinates a blended person.

contentBody:
Four replies land on a “hold my mess token” flow:

- Two people cannot see whether the roommate opened, accepted, or paid after the request.
- One asks for sticker rewards that are not on the screen.
- One never skips meals and does not need the product.

Which judgement is correct?
option.1: Claim “users want this” because two people liked the idea, and ship sticker rewards in the same pass as proof of demand.
option.2: Average all four voices into one score out of 10, then build a lending arm because someone might think a token hold is a loan.
option.3: Treat the missing post-request trail as a finding — it stalled twice — park invented rewards, and leave the person who never skips meals out of the MVP story.
option.4: Ignore the repeated stall and rebuild the whole product around the one person who asked for stickers that were never shown.
answerExplanation:
A finding is a repeated stall or confusion you trust enough to act on — a pattern, not a popularity score. If two people cannot see how the request proceeds, the trail after “request sent” is the problem. One person asking for stickers that are not on the screen is invented; ignore it. A person who never has the pain is a wrong user; thank them and stop recruiting them. You can claim the trail is unclear. You should not claim “users want this.”

**Why other options are wrong:**
- A: Likes are not evidence of the job. Rewards that were not on the screen are not a Now item.
- B: Scores hide where people get lost. One loan-fear comment is not a reason to build a lending product.
- D: Acting on a single invented extra, while ignoring a stall that appeared twice, is the reverse of pattern-spotting.

contentBody:
Neha is writing tests for “ask a friend to pay the photocopy-shop bill when you are stuck in a viva.”

Which of the following are correct?
option.1: A strong scenario still needs who, when and where, what they want, what they see or miss, and the risk if it fails.
option.2: PQRSTU helps invent holistic “how well” tests, but she still selects which rows are must-have now; it is not a day-one shopping list.
option.3: “Would you use this in future?” and “Do you like this?” are enough, because polite yes answers prove the intended problem is solved.
option.4: Security means “is it fast enough in the moment that matters,” and Performance means “can a stranger or a scam use this against someone.”
answerExplanation:
You cannot invent a useful test from a slogan. A solid scenario answers who (and mood), when and where, what they want, what they see or miss, and the risk if it fails. Functional needs say what the product must do. PQRSTU (Performance, Quality/scale, Reliability, Security, Transparency, Usability) asks how well. Not every row ships in version one. When she writes the MVP card, she stars the rows that must be true now and leaves the rest as later tests, not as secret promises on the page.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- C: Those questions invite polite fiction. They do not test the intended job (complete this photocopy payment while you are in the viva).
- D: Those two letters are reversed. Performance is speed in the moment that matters. Security is whether a stranger or a scam can use the flow against someone.

contentBody:
Farhan simulated three voices for a parcel-desk page. One comment says a roommate collected the parcel in person and the page never updated. One comment asks for rewards points that are not on the screen. One comment says “I will not ask a roommate — self-respect.”

Which of the following are correct?
option.1: Simulated replies are plausible reactions, not real evidence, real money fear, or proof that a friend will actually pay.
option.2: If the same stall appears on two voices, treat it as a likely product issue and a candidate for Now; if it appears once, confirm with a real person.
option.3: Cross out any comment that names a feature not on the screen, and never treat “I would tap yes” as a completed payment.
option.4: Because a practical mix is about 60% simulated, he can skip real people and publish chatbot scores as a survey of India.
answerExplanation:
AI is a fast rehearsal. It sees the path you pasted, understands your intent too easily, invents features, has no real money on the line, is weak on real alternatives, and wants to please you. Simulation is good for rehearsing questions and spotting obvious confusion. It cannot prove demand or trust. A repeated stall across two voices is a likely Now issue. A one-off needs a real person. Invented extras (rewards not on the screen) get deleted. “I would tap yes” is not a payment.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- D: The 40% real / 60% simulated mix is simulation for volume and real people for truth. Do not invert it. Do not call the chatbot a field study or publish scores as a survey.

contentBody:
Kavya’s prototype lets a student ask a roommate to pay the Wi-Fi bill. Testers send the request easily, then ask: did they open it, accept, reject, or pay? Some fear it is a loan. Auto-detecting a Google Pay payment needs extra plumbing. Multi-party net settlement impressed one person and is heavy to explain.

Which of the following are correct?
option.1: Put a visible status trail and “settle later, not a loan” copy in Now — they block understanding or trust and can ship in this pass.
option.2: Put multi-party net settlement and a lending or rewards arm in Now, because impressive extras protect the core job in version one.
option.3: Put other-app detection in Next; park lending, rewards, disputes, and multi-beneficiary settlement as Later or outside this MVP.
option.4: An MVP must include every payment method, automatic cash detection, and a social feed, or it is not viable.
answerExplanation:
Prioritisation ranks changes by how much they protect the core job, how much effort they take, and whether they fit the MVP. Now is for blockers you can ship in this pass: the status trail after the request, and copy that this is settle later, not a loan. Next is for trust or coverage that needs real users or more plumbing — including payments made in another app. Later is extra complexity only a few voices asked for: lending, rewards, friend-vs-friend disputes, multi-beneficiary net settlement. An MVP is the smallest offer that delivers the core value and lets you learn. It includes the request, a clear status until paid, and a path if someone declines. It does not include loans, rewards, a social feed, credit score, multi-beneficiary settlement, or every manual / multi-app path.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- B: Impressive extras with heavy cognitive load do not belong in version one. Lending is a different product and feeds the exact confusion testers already have.
- D: Viable can mean a manual backstage (you confirm a cash payment yourself) as long as you do not pretend the system already sees every rupee. Building everything is the failure mode.

contentBody:
Imran found that people understand “send request” but not the trail after it. One simulated voice asked for rewards. A real tester could not tell if the roommate paid. He must iterate once and then present.

Which of the following are correct?
option.1: Change the smallest thing that retests the stall — a four-step status trail plus an escape hatch — then recheck the same five questions; do not invent a lending arm because one voice said “loan.”
option.2: Treat the simulated voices as a survey, skip the change log, and end with a twelve-item roadmap instead of one ask to try request → status → paid or declined.
option.3: Fill an MVP card with the core job, who and when, includes, excludes, and how he will know it is working enough to learn.
option.4: When presenting, give a rationale and a change log that labels real versus simulated sources; real user findings outrank simulated ones if they compete; name the trade-off and the open risk.
answerExplanation:
Iteration is a bounded change in response to a finding, then a recheck of the same questions. The missing trail is the hypothesis: request sent and delivered; roommate opened and agreed; payment in progress; paid — plus a way to message them, ask someone else, pay yourself, or cancel. Do not add loans or rewards. An MVP card locks the smallest offer and the learning check (a tester can follow request → status → paid or declined without asking “did it work?”). Presentation is a clear account: who and the intended problem, what the first prototype offered, what you heard (label simulated vs real), what you changed, what you parked and why, what you will build or test next. A rationale is why a change or a cut serves the user and the MVP. A change log maps each edit or refusal to a finding and a source. A trade-off is the downside you accepted on purpose (simple request plus trail, not a full settlement and lending system). Real user findings outrank simulated ones when they compete. End with one ask, not a twelve-item roadmap.

**Why other options are wrong:**
- B: Simulated voices are not a survey. Skipping the change log hides sources. A long roadmap is not the close. If you treat simulation as a census, rewrite that sentence.
